newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Pru boosts coffers as SwissRe buys M&G.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Pru boosts coffers as SwissRe buys M&G.

text.p: British life and pensions giant Prudential sold its Mercantile & General reinsurance business to Swiss Re for 1.75 billion pounds ($2.73 billion) on Tuesday, boosting an already bulging acquisition war chest.
The group said on Tuesday that Swiss Re, which sold M&G to Prudential nearly 30 years ago, had been one of a limited number of buyers attracted to the global life and health reinsurer.
Reinsurance is one of the world's biggest and least known financial service industries, in which companies underwrite insurance sold by others for a portion of the premium paid.
Seeking to raise funds for further expansion in other areas of financial services, Prudential had announced in June that it planned to float a substantial part of M&G later this year.

But the offer from Swiss Re outstripped the value placed on M&G by analysts, most of whom had suspected a trade sale was still very much a possibility. All of it bar 50 million pounds is cash, and Prudential is well funded for an acquisition spree to build on its presence in Britain, the United States and Asia.
It has for some time been looking to buy either a building society or life assurer in Britain. But group chief executive Peter Davis told Reuters he was in no hurry to spend the money.
"We certainly won't be rushed into doing something simply because we now have greater availability of funds," said Davis.

"If the right opportunity presents itself at a sensible price and we can demonstrate value to our shareholders, then we'll do it," he said, but added the pace of change in the life assurance industry and among mutual building societies was slow.
Shares in Prudential edged three pence higher to 440p. On the Zurich bourse, Swiss Re was up 22 Swiss francs at 1292.
Davis confirmed the group had pursued a twin track approach to M&G, with sale or flotation dependent on several factors.
"It was always a serious intention of ours to float the M&G, unless one of the trade buyers particularly wanted to buy it."
"But with a limited number of buyers and with other rationalisation going on, the timing might not have been right or someone may have already done something else."
Swiss Re earlier this month lost out to Munich Re in a bid battle for U.S. property and casualty reinsurer American Re. Its bigger rival paid $3.3 billion or over three times book value.

While M&G is by no means a substitute, analysts said the purchase fitted with Swiss Re's strategy of expanding into targeted niche areas. They said of the timing that Swiss Re would have had its hands full if it had bought American Re.

One analyst estimated the price paid was between 12 and 13 times net earnings, but said this was not exorbitant given the size and market position of M&G, which saw pre-tax profits of 326 million pounds last year on 1.3 billion premium income.
After the acquisition is completed by the end of this year, Swiss Re will be the largest life and health reinsurer in the world. It bought the smaller Dutch reinsurer Alhermij last year.
"When people look at demographics and the needs of life insurers, it's a good growth area," said Roman Cizdyn, analyst at Merrill Lynch. "I think the stock market float did chivvy things up."

The deal is further evidence of the rapid consolidation taking place in the reinsurance industry worldwide. U.S.-based Employers Re was also cited by some analysts as a possible buyer for M&G and may turn its sights on an alternative acquisition.

"The consolidation is being driven from two sides," said Brian Shea of Salomon Brothers. "The sellers of reinsurance are noting that having a seamless worldwide business makes a lot of sense and there's a lot of back office synergies. The purchasers of reinsurance are asking for better capitalised companies."
U.S. direct reinsurer General Re's purchase of National Re for $940 million in July heralded the last two months of upheaval, and the consolidation is expected to spread to Europe.
